summary: Defines MIB objects for managing AppleTalk networks with SNMP. It was written on the standards track but is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of gauges for checking on networks that use Apple's old networking system.

questions: how to manage appletalk with snmp
subtitle: SNMP management objects for AppleTalk networks, extending RFC 1243 up to the transport and session layers.

tldr.problem: As large AppleTalk networks were built alongside large IP networks, there was a need to manage AppleTalk with SNMP, and RFC 1243 covered only the layers up to the network layer.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the APPLETALK-MIB module, organized into 18 groups, adding groups for transport and session protocols and extra variables for the lower layers, in an upwardly compatible way.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 1243 and was written on the standards track, but its status is now Historic.

today: RFC 1742 is now Historic. It obsoleted RFC 1243, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
AppleTalk is a protocol suite with an open peer-to-peer architecture that runs over many media, and it interoperates with IP through encapsulation methods. This MIB defines managed objects so AppleTalk networks can be managed with SNMP. RFC 1243 defined objects for the lower layers, up to the network layer. This memo adds objects for the transport and session layers, plus extensions to the lower layers, and it obsoletes RFC 1243.

The Network Management Framework it builds on is the SMI (RFC 1155), the concise description format (RFC 1212), MIB-I and MIB-II, and SNMP (RFC 1157). The objects are defined in ASN.1 using the SMI subset.
sections.plainLanguage: An older list of gauges covered only the bottom floors of a building. This one adds the upper floors too.

sections.title: The Eighteen Groups
sections.content:
Objects sit under appletalk, which is { mib-2 13 }, and are arranged in groups: LLAP, AARP, ATPort, DDP, DDP Router, RTMP, RTMP Stub, KIP, ZIP Router, ZIP End Node, NBP, ATEcho, ATP, PAP, ASP, ADSP, ATPortPtoP and Per Port Counters.

Groups are the basic unit of conformance. If a group's semantics apply to an implementation, it must implement all objects in that group. For example, an agent must implement the KIP group if and only if it implements the KIP protocol.

The groups follow the stack. Examples: LLAP manages LocalTalk links, AARP maps AppleTalk node addresses to data-link addresses, DDP is the network-layer datagram protocol, RTMP maintains routing tables, NBP converts human-readable service names to network addresses, ATP supports transactions, PAP links workstations and print servers, and ADSP provides connection-oriented, full-duplex communication between two sockets.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges are sorted into labelled drawers, one for each job the network does. A device only needs the drawers for the jobs it actually does.

sections.title: Additions and Changes from RFC 1243
sections.content:
Nine new groups are introduced: DDP Router, RTMP Stub, ZIP Router, ATP, PAP, ASP, ADSP, ATPortPtoP and Per Port Counters. Many variables, mostly counters, were added to existing groups, for example aarpLookups and aarpHits, extra RTMP counters, and several NBP counters.

Four LLAP variables (llapInPkts, llapOutPkts, llapInNoHandlers, llapInErrors) are deprecated because the interfaces table of MIB-II duplicates them. Other changes include splitting the DDP group in two (one part for any node, one for routers only), renaming the ZIP group to ZIP End Node, making atportNetConfig and atportZoneConfig read-write, and adding the enumeration invalid(5) to rtmpState for deleting rows.
sections.plainLanguage: The new edition adds many new gauges and retires four that were copies of gauges found elsewhere.

sections.title: Textual Conventions
sections.content:
Four new data types are introduced as textual conventions. They only make the document easier to read and do not change the syntax or meaning of the objects.

  • ATNetworkNumber: an octet string of 2 octets, network byte order.
  • DdpNodeAddress: 3 octets, a 2-octet network number then 1 octet of node number.
  • DdpSocketAddress: 4 octets, network, node and a 1-octet socket number (0..255).
  • ATName: 0 to 32 octets of AppleTalk ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: These are standard shapes for writing down an address, like agreeing that a street address always has a number, a street and a town in the same order.

sections.title: Definitions and Security
sections.content:
Section 5, which fills most of the memo's 84 pages, holds the full APPLETALK-MIB definitions: every object with its syntax, access and description. It imports Counter, IpAddress and TimeTicks from RFC1155-SMI, DisplayString and mib-2 from RFC1213-MIB, and OBJECT-TYPE from RFC-1212. The registry-style definitions include object identifiers for forwarding protocols and for point-to-point protocols such as AURP.

The memo states that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the pages are the exact definition of every gauge. The memo does not say anything about keeping the gauges safe from snoopers.
